hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

assessments.reason: Self-restarting Skype app with WerFault crash.
Packed python dropped via PsExec, spawns conhost/cmd/powershell and opens LSASS.
Password-protected Rar of credential-hunting archive, then sdelete'd.
Anti-forensic deletion of Rar.exe and working.zip.
Attacker-staged Sysinternals tool run from PowerShell for permission recon.
Used with cleartext password to launch python.exe on NASHUA.
Anti-forensic wiping of payload and archives.
Masqueraded screen-saver payload launched from explorer, later sdelete'd.
Compiles attacker C# from PowerShell temp dirs into DLLs.
Rare binary started by PowerShell on scranton.
UAC-bypass-capable binary spawned by cmd under pbeesly.

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, use of Windows Credential Manager APIs, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of any credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or registry hives, and no anomalous credential-related events on the compromised Windows hosts.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: Full-access LSASS handle from wsmprovhost on nashua.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: Only lsass.exe touched HKLM\SAM and SAM_SERVER/SAM_DOMAIN objects; no non-lsass SAM access, no reg save/hive copy, no SAM dump files.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No NTDS file creation, ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow command lines or shadow-copy messages in any dataset.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No lsadump/secrets command lines, no SECURITY\Policy\Secrets object access, no LSA/Secrets strings in PowerShell or windows.other.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes were performed by lsass.exe itself (normal cached-credential updates); no other process read or exported the cache.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No drsuapi/dcsync/lsadump references in process command lines or PowerShell script blocks; lateral movement used PsExec with explicit credentials, not directory replication.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: No network sniffing artifacts in any dataset: no tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap execution (sysmon 1 and security 4688 stacks), no pcap/sniff/promiscuous command lines or PowerShell script blocks, no Npcap/WinPcap driver image loads (sysmon 6) and no capture-driver service installs (7045). The only capture-capable binary is Microsoft's signed Azure Network Watcher agent installed by the Azure guest agent extension on scranton (benign platform provisioning). The attacker's python.exe on nashua is a C2/exfil client to 192.168.0.4:8443, not a sniffer. Zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window and shows only normal service ports plus self-signed-cert notices.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Input capture via keystrokes and clipboard.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No IIS/wwwroot/login file or process activity and no HTTP POST or login/portal URLs; checks C084/C086/C087/C089/C091 returned zero hits.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: Credential API access via full-access LSASS handles.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625 failed logons and zero 4740 lockouts in windows.security; the only 4776 is a success (0x0). No authentication-failure burst exists.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No 4625 events, no password-bearing process command lines, no Password/Credential strings in PowerShell 4104 blocks.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No cracking tooling, wordlists or potfiles were seen, but LSASS was opened with 0x1FFFFF by PowerShell on scranton at 03:05:16Z and an obfuscated reflective shellcode loader ran at 23:21:29 local — credential extraction from memory that would feed offline cracking. Mapped to T1110.002 as the closest allowed technique; the underlying activity is LSASS credential dumping.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: Only one user account (pbeesly) authenticates; no failures, no lockouts, no user-list spray tooling.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed logons and no external credential source; 4648 events are internal re-use of pbeesly's own credentials.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smart-card/token-provider interception artifacts. The Credential* registry hits are routine Credential Guard configuration (Enabled=0x00000000 by lsass.exe, Wininit event 14 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0') and standard CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service creation by services.exe. LSASS access is overwhelmingly svchost.exe 0x1000 and Azure antimalware 0x1400; the only full-access handles are the attacker's own PowerShell (scranton 03:05:16) and wsmprovhost (nashua 03:09:29) sessions. The 4648 events are pbeesly re-logon via PSEXESVC.exe on nashua and system DWM/UMFD logons on scranton. The real credential activity is plaintext password reuse in a PsExec64.exe command line, which is credential access but not MFA interception.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: LSASS full-access handles from PowerShell/WinRM hosts.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No browser cookie database was read or copied (only a benign svchost INetCookies cache write), but on scranton.dmevals.local a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell stager (payload decoded from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png) opened MicrosoftEdge.exe, MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe and MicrosoftEdgeSH.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:05:17 — full access to browser processes, the standard mechanism for extracting session cookies from browser memory. The DavSetCookie/WebDAV hits are benign client behaviour. Cookie theft is strongly indicated but the stolen cookie content itself is not directly observable in the telemetry.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Cleartext passwords used in PsExec and WebDAV exfil.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Password/login/vpn file collection archived on nashua.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All 17 Password/Credential registry value sets come from svchost.exe, lsass.exe, services.exe and winlogon.exe performing normal OS/service configuration.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No process-creation or object-access events referencing consolehost_history or PowerShell history files.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: No sysvol/groups.xml or cpassword access found; only routine GroupPolicy DataStore writes of GptTmpl.inf/gpt.ini.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: No Credential Manager or vault extraction seen.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: All browser-credential checks (C209-C214) returned zero hits; only normal MicrosoftEdge.exe writes to its own AppContainer DataStore were seen.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: All password-manager checks (C221-C226) returned zero hits; Rar.exe archiving of *pass*/*login* files is generic collection, not password-manager store access.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: Full-access LSASS handles (0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF) from PowerShell.exe on scranton and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua indicate credential-theft tooling touching the authentication process, but no actual modification of LSASS/authentication components was observed.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: 4624 type-3 logons are machine-account/loopback traffic and 4648 logons are PsExec/winlogon; no 5136/4739 DC authentication changes.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No Notification Packages/PasswordFilter registry writes, no password-filter DLL drops, only Microsoft-signed auth DLL loads.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/5136 policy changes and no MFA-related cmdlets in PowerShell logs.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: Certificate private keys exported for trust abuse.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider/Credential registry writes or PowerShell references to network provider DLLs.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No AiTM positioning: Sysmon 3 destination hostnames all '-', DNS queries only routine AD/telemetry lookups, wpad.dmevals.local answered NXDOMAIN by the DC. The intrusion present (PsExec64 with plaintext password to NASHUA, javamtsup service, python.exe to 192.168.0.4:8443) is lateral movement/credential use, not AiTM.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay. 4697 events are Windows per-user service registrations plus PSEXESVC and javamtsup installs; 5140/5145 show only normal machine-account IPC$/SYSVOL/samr/lsarpc and pbeesly's ADMIN$ PsExec access.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: Only three source and three responder MACs in Zeek conn data; the unusual responder 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a placeholder MAC used consistently, with no duplicate MAC-to-IP mapping or gratuitous ARP pattern.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP event codes in windows.other, no DHCP PowerShell content, no Sysmon connections to ports 67/68, and the Zeek capture contains no dhcp log type, so DHCP spoofing cannot be seen and nothing indicates it.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: Credential-access precursor confirmed on scranton (obfuscated PowerShell shellcode loader by pbeesly) and full-access LSASS handles from PowerShell.exe (0x1f3fff/0x1fffff) and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua (0x1f3fff), but no forged/abused Kerberos ticket artefacts were found.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: All 28 4769 tickets AES256 (0x12), krbtgt tickets only for pbeesly and SCRANTON$ machine account, no RC4 downgrade or anomalous 4672 logons.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: Service tickets requested only for computer accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) with Status 0x0 and AES256; no forged service tickets.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No RC4 service-ticket requests, no SPN user accounts targeted, no Kerberoast/Rubeus script blocks.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: AS exchange required pre-authentication (KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED then AES256 success); no AS-REP roasting tooling in PowerShell logs.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: Real credential-access activity on scranton.dmevals.local: pbeesly's PowerShell toolkit exported all LocalMachine certificates with private keys to .pfx (Get-PrivateKeys, hardcoded password "saribas"), PowerShell.exe opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF, and exfil/cleanup functions plus PsExec with cleartext credentials to NASHUA were used. This is a credible precursor to forging web credentials, but no forged credential was observed.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only benign cookie artifacts: a service-profile INetCookies file created by svchost.exe and standard WebDAV davclnt.dll DavSetCookie calls to 192.168.0.4. No browser cookie theft or forged cookie use in any dataset.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: No SAML/Assertion/NotOnOrAfter strings in PowerShell, no saml/token/cert command lines in Sysmon, and no saml/adfs/token HTTP URLs in Zeek. Certificate export is a precursor only; no token forging or use was seen.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA/2FA/authenticator/push/OTP artifacts in PowerShell 4104 script blocks, sysmon process command lines, security logon events or zeek HTTP URLs. The C355 windows.other hits are routine WMI provider start/DeleteInstance records from wmiprvse.exe (5857/5858) on newyork.dmevals.local, and the only authentication-failure-family security event is a successful NTLM validation (4776, Error Code 0x0) for pbeesly — no repeated authentication prompts or MFA fatigue pattern. The hosts do show unrelated malicious activity (PsExec64 with plaintext credentials to NASHUA, C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, sdelete64 wiping archives, hidden base64/gzip PowerShell on scranton), but none of it is MFA request generation.

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot credential-dumping tools (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll rundll32) among rare executables.
Stack process-access targets to find LSASS or other credential-store processes being opened.
Stack object types accessed under handle/object-access auditing to find SAM/SECURITY/LSASS objects.
Stack newly created processes to spot dumping utilities launched on hosts.

args.query: event.code:4104 AND (powershell.script_block_text:*lsass* OR powershell.script_block_text:*mimikatz* OR powershell.script_block_text:*sekurlsa* OR powershell.script_block_text:*DumpCreds*)

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell script blocks referencing LSASS/credential-dumping APIs.
Look for credential-dumping references in other Windows event channels (service installs, VSS, etc.).
Stack granted-access masks on LSASS process opens to reveal memory-read access typical of dumping.
Read individual LSASS access events with source image and granted access.

findings.title: Credential-access toolchain staged by pbeesly: Sysinternals, accesschk, private-key export, PsExec to NASHUA, packed python.exe, Rar archive
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local pbeesly expanded SysinternalsSuite.zip into C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite, ran accesschk.exe, defined and invoked a Get-PrivateKeys function that exports every LocalMachine certificate to a random .pfx in Downloads, and used sdelete64.exe to wipe artifacts (C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr, Draft.Zip, SysinternalsSuite.zip). From 03:11:18 to 03:14:42 UTC pbeesly launched PsExec64.exe four times against \\NASHUA with the cleartext password Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by to run C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe. On nashua.dmevals.local PSEXESVC.exe spawned that python.exe (PyInstaller bundle unpacking _ssl.pyd, pywintypes27.dll, _hashlib.pyd into _MEI29522), which made hundreds of outbound connections to 192.168.0.4:8443, spawned cmd.exe, and Rar.exe created a password-protected archive C:\Users\pbeesly\Desktop\working.zip; sdelete64.exe then wiped Rar.exe and working.zip. This is a hands-on credential-theft and exfiltration chain, and it is the context for the LSASS memory reads reported under T1003.001.
PsExec64 with cleartext creds launched python.exe on NASHUA; sdelete64 wiped the victim payload and archives.
findings.title: Sysinternals credential-access toolchain executed by pbeesly
pbeesly PowerShell requests full-access handle to LSASS on scranton and nashua
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16 UTC the account pbeesly (DMEVALS, SID ...-1107) running C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe on scranton.dmevals.local requested a handle to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1FFFFF, which the audit message expands to 'Read from process memory' / 'Write to process memory' / 'Duplicate handle into or out of process' — the classic LSASS memory-read pattern used by dumping tools. A second handle with 0x1F3FFF was requested in the same second, and Sysmon corroborates the same source image (PowerShell.exe) opening lsass with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 03:05:16. At 03:09:29 UTC the same user, via wsmprovhost.exe (WinRM) on nashua.dmevals.local, again opened lsass with 0x1F3FFF (Sysmon GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff). This is preceded by pbeesly unpacking SysinternalsSuite, running accesschk.exe, and a PowerShell 'Get-PrivateKeys' function that exports certificates to .pfx files, i.e. an active credential-theft toolchain. The only other LSASS opens in the window are svchost/wininit/csrss/AntimalwareConfig/CollectGuestLogs with 0x1000/0x1400/0x101001 masks, which are normal.

findings.title: PowerShell and WinRM-host processes opened LSASS with full-access rights on scranton and nashua
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02, 326 Sysmon event-10 records show processes accessing lsass.exe. Stacking by GrantedAccess/SourceImage shows the bulk is benign (svchost.exe 286x at 0x1000, Azure antimalware/telemetry at 0x1400). The rare outliers are attacker-relevant: on scranton.dmevals.local PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with 0x1F3FFF at 03:05:16.623Z and with 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16.654Z, and on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, a WinRM remote-PowerShell host) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29.430Z. The wsmprovhost call trace runs through Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, i.e. a PowerShell cmdlet performed the access. These are full-access LSASS handles from scripting hosts, consistent with credential theft tooling rather than normal system behaviour. No evidence of an actual authentication-process modification (no LSASS image-load of a non-Microsoft DLL, no registry write to LSASS/SAM/msv1_0, no service/DLL registration) was found, so the T1556 family itself is not confirmed as modified authentication.

The high-mask LSASS handles are therefore suspicious but not confirmed password-store theft; the surrounding activity is clearly malicious credential-adjacent collection (keystrokes, clipboard, private keys).

findings.title: LSASS handle stacking: rare full-access masks from PowerShell/wsmprovhost, but no Credential Manager or DPAPI vault access
findings.summary: Stacking the 326 Sysmon event-10 handles on lsass.exe shows 293 with 0x1000 and 24 with 0x1400 (routine svchost/Azure telemetry/antimalware), plus rare outliers: 0x1fffff (3), 0x1f3fff (2), 0x101001 (2), 0x1000000 (1), 0x3000 (1). The 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff handles come from PowerShell.exe on scranton (03:05:16) and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua (03:09:29) under pbeesly; the 0x101001 handles come from svchost.exe with an lsm.dll call trace (normal LSA plumbing) and 0x1fffff also from wininit/csrss at boot. Security 4663/4656 auditing shows the same pbeesly PowerShell/wsmprovhost access to lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff. No cmdkey/vaultcmd usage, no Credential Manager vault file or registry access, and no DPAPI Protect-blob access by a non-system process was found; the only 'vault'/'credential' registry hits were services.exe MuiCache and CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service registration, and Credential Guard was reported disabled (0x0) on scranton. Suspicious LSASS access, but Credential Manager theft is not evidenced.

findings.title: SAM hive registry access on scranton by lsass only; no attacker SAM dump observed
findings.summary: The only SAM-related registry activity in the window is lsass.exe itself touching HKLM\SAM\SAM\RXACT and HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:19:10 UTC, and the only SAM_SERVER/SAM_DOMAIN/SAM_ALIAS handle requests are made by lsass.exe under the machine account SCRANTON$ (e.g. SAM_SERVER 'SAM' AccessMask 0xf003f). No non-lsass process requested SAM objects, no 'reg save' / hive-copy command lines were found, and the only file-create hits matching SAM/SECURITY were Prefetch .pf files. This is normal local SAM maintenance, not credential dumping.

findings.title: No NTDS / volume-shadow credential dumping observed
findings.summary: No hits were returned for NTDS file creation, ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow command lines, or shadow-copy related messages in sysmon, security, powershell or windows.other. The only vssvc.exe activity seen was as a process-access target, not a shadow-copy creation by attacker tooling. Nothing in the retrieved data supports domain-database theft.

findings.title: No LSA Secrets / lsadump activity observed
findings.summary: Searches for 'secrets', 'lsadump', 'reg save HKLM\SECURITY' in process command lines, for SECURITY\Policy\Secrets object access, and for LSA/Secrets strings in PowerShell script blocks and windows.other messages returned no hits. The SECURITY hive touches that were found are lsass writing HKLM\SECURITY\RXACT and HKLM\SECURITY\Cache, which is normal LSA behaviour.

findings.title: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache (NL$) writes by lsass on nashua/scranton — normal cached-credential updates
findings.summary: Sysmon registry-set events on HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 were recorded on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:11:40, 03:12:46, 03:13:49 and 03:15:03 UTC and on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:20:46 UTC, all with Image C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe and Details 'Binary Data'. These are the LSA writing cached domain credential entries itself; no other process read or exported the SECURITY\Cache key, and no PowerShell script block referenced cache/DCC2/mscache. Note the timing coincides with the attacker's PsExec/python activity on nashua, but the writes are performed by lsass, not by the attacker tooling.

findings.title: No DCSync / DRSUAPI replication abuse observed
findings.summary: No process command lines or PowerShell script blocks referencing drsuapi, dcsync or lsadump were found in sysmon or powershell. The attacker's lateral movement used PsExec64.exe with explicit credentials (\\NASHUA -u dmevals\pbeesly -p ...) and a PyInstaller-packed python.exe, not directory replication. No evidence of DCSync in the retrieved data.

findings.title: No network sniffing observed; Azure Network Watcher agent install is benign platform activity
findings.summary: The only capture-capable component seen is Microsoft's Azure Network Watcher agent on scranton.dmevals.local. It was started as a service by services.exe at 2020-05-02T03:19:13Z and then Test/Install/Start'd at 03:20:41-03:20:42Z by cmd.exe running the Azure guest-agent extension script C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\enable.cmd, whose parent is C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\GuestAgent\WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe (SYSTEM). This is the standard Azure VM extension provisioning path, signed by 'Microsoft CoreXT', and no Npcap/WinPcap driver load (sysmon event 6) or pcap service install (7045) was found. No tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap execution and no pcap/sniff/promiscuous command lines or script blocks were observed.

findings.title: No keylogger indicators found
findings.summary: No process creation or PowerShell script block referencing keylogging APIs (GetAsyncKeyState, SetWindowsHookEx, keylog) was found; the dedicated checks returned zero hits. The LSASS/winlogon process-access events observed are handle opens by svchost.exe (0x1000), wininit.exe/csrss.exe (0x1fffff at boot 03:19:09Z) and the malicious PowerShell/python described above, not a keyboard-hook implant.

findings.title: No GUI credential-prompt capture observed
findings.summary: No 4688 process creation or PowerShell script block matching Credential/prompt/Read-Host was found (checks C076/C080 returned zero hits). The only 'prompt' script blocks are the normal interactive PowerShell prompt strings in pbeesly's session on scranton and nashua.

findings.title: No web portal capture observed
findings.summary: No file writes to wwwroot/inetpub/login paths, no w3wp/IIS command lines, no 4663 access to web content and no HTTP POST or login/portal URLs in the zeek window were found (checks C084/C086/C087/C089/C091 all zero hits). The only web-related activity is rundll32 davclnt.dll DavSetCookie to http://192.168.0.4/webdav on scranton, which is WebDAV client access, not a credential-capturing portal.

Across windows.security (2020-05-02T02:55:25Z..03:28:09Z) there are zero 4625 failed-logon events and zero 4740 lockouts; the only 4776 credential validation is a success (Status 0x0) for pbeesly from workstation 10.0.1.4 on newyork.dmevals.local at 23:20:40 local. 4624 logons are 297 total, dominated by machine-account network logons (NEWYORK$ 123, SCRANTON$ 37, NASHUA$ 25) and SYSTEM service logons, with only pbeesly as an interactive user. The 4648 explicit-credential events (15) are pbeesly re-using its own credentials via PSEXESVC.exe on nashua and svchost/winlogon on scranton, plus DWM/UMFD/SCRANTON$ system logons — lateral movement with already-known credentials, not guessing. No authentication-failure burst exists to support any T1110 sub-technique.
findings.title: No brute-force authentication activity; credential theft occurred via LSASS access instead

findings.summary: No 4625 events exist in windows.security, so there is no sequence of failed authentications against any account. Sysmon process-creation events with 'password' in the command line returned nothing, and PowerShell 4104 script blocks contained no Password/Credential strings. The only authentication-related PowerShell activity is an obfuscated reflective loader (see T1110.002 finding), which is credential theft, not guessing.
findings.title: No password guessing: zero 4625 failures and no password-bearing command lines

findings.summary: Only one user account (pbeesly) appears in 4624/4648/4776 authentication events; there is no spread of one password across many accounts and no 4625 failures or 4740 lockouts that spraying would produce. The 4648 events on nashua.dmevals.local show pbeesly's own credentials being passed to PSEXESVC.exe for remote execution, and the sysmon command-line stack for '*user*' returned only C:\windows\system32\userinit.exe. No spray tooling or user lists were observed.
findings.title: No password spraying: single account, no failures, no user-list tooling

findings.summary: There are no 4625 failed logons in windows.security, so no stuffing attempt (which requires many rejected credential pairs) is visible. The only credential-validation record is a successful 4776 for pbeesly from 10.0.1.4, and the 4648 events are internal re-use of pbeesly's credentials. Credential-related messages in windows.other are benign system records (Credential Guard configuration 0x0 on scranton, SAM remote-call security descriptor notice). The stolen-credential activity on these hosts is LSASS memory access, not stuffing.
findings.title: No credential stuffing: no failed logons and no external credential source
No MFA/smart-card interception observed; credential theft on scranton/nashua is plaintext password reuse via PsExec, not MFA bypass
findings.summary: The T1111 check hits are explained by benign Windows behaviour plus a non-MFA credential-access chain. (1) The only 'Credential*' registry writes are routine: lsass.exe setting HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled to DWORD (0x00000000) on scranton at 2020-05-02T03:19:09.865Z (Credential Guard not enabled, matching the Wininit event 14 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' on the same host at 03:19:09), and services.exe creating the standard CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc_13619b service keys on scranton (03:20:48) and MuiCache entries on nashua (03:21:58). (2) LSASS handle access (Sysmon 10) is dominated by svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (216 on scranton, 30 newyork, 28 nashua, 12 utica) and Azure antimalware/telemetry processes with 0x1400; the rare full-access handles (0x1f3ffff/0x1fffff) come from PowerShell.exe on scranton at 03:05:16 and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua at 03:09:29, i.e. the attacker's own PowerShell/WinRM session, not an MFA token provider. (3) The 4648 explicit-credential logons are pbeesly re-authenticating to NASHUA through PSEXESVC.exe (localhost target, 4 times between 03:11:40 and 03:15:03) plus DWM/UMFD/winlogon/taskhostw system logons on scranton. The driving activity is a plaintext password ('Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by') passed on the PsExec64.exe command line from scranton to \\NASHUA, with C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe launched as a child of PSEXESVC.exe on nashua — credential reuse, not MFA interception. No smart-card, token-provider, or MFA-related script block was found (the 4104 search for Credential/MFA/token/lsass/sekurlsa/smartcard returned only the attacker's image-steganography loader, an Invoke-Exfil function, and benign AD/script resource modules).

findings.title: SMB share access events (5140/5145) are domain-controller SYSVOL replication, not forced authentication
findings.summary: The 163 events matching 5140/5145 are machine-account access to the SYSVOL share on newyork.dmevals.local: NEWYORK$ from its own link-local IPv6 address fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 and SCRANTON$ from 10.0.1.4, all with Share Name \\*\SYSVOL and Share Path \??\F:\SYSVOL\sysvol. These are normal DFSR/Group Policy replication reads by domain controllers (matching the DFSR config XML and GptTmpl.inf file transfers seen in Zeek), not inbound authentication coerced from a victim. The corresponding Sysmon 3 SMB connections to 10.0.0.4/10.0.1.6 are System process (PID 4) kernel SMB traffic between DCs. No user-account SMB authentication to an external or unusual host was observed.

findings.title: DavSetCookie rundll32 invocations on scranton.dmevals.local are WebDAV client behaviour, not cookie theft
findings.summary: Five 4688 events on scranton.dmevals.local show rundll32.exe C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav, spawned by svchost.exe under the pbeesly logon. This is the standard Windows WebDAV redirector (davclnt) storing a WebDAV auth cookie for the share http://192.168.0.4/webdav — it writes a cookie, it does not steal one. The matching network view (zeek, non-overlapping window) shows the same WebDAV client user agent Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362 from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4:80 retrieving /webdav/python.exe (401 then 200, application/x-dosexec, 5305104 bytes), i.e. a WebDAV file download rather than cookie exfiltration. The only cookie-named file creation in the whole window is svchost.exe writing C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\...\AC\INetCookies, a normal WinINet cache artifact.

findings.title: Registry Password/Credential value sets are OS service activity, not credential theft
findings.summary: The 17 Sysmon 13 hits on Password/Credential registry paths are all written by legitimate Windows components: svchost.exe setting HKU\.DEFAULT\Software\Microsoft\IdentityCRL\ProviderPasswordLength/CharacterGroups on nashua and scranton, lsass.exe setting DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled, and services.exe creating the CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc_13619b service keys plus winlogon.exe writing PasswordExpiryNotification\NotShownTime. No attacker process read or wrote credential stores in the registry.

findings.title: No Group Policy Preferences credential access observed
findings.summary: Searches for sysvol/groups.xml access in Sysmon process creation, Security object access and windows.other returned no hits. The only GPP-related file activity is the legitimate GroupPolicy DataStore write of GptTmpl.inf and gpt.ini under C:\Windows\System32\GroupPolicy\DataStore\0\sysvol\dmevals.local, which is normal policy refresh, not cpassword harvesting.

findings.title: No browser credential-store access observed
findings.summary: Checks C209-C214 returned zero hits: no process command line referencing Login Data, logins.json or browser profile paths, no file creation of browser credential files, no process-access events against chrome.exe/firefox.exe, no object-access auditing on browser credential files, and no PowerShell or other-channel references. The only browser-related activity retrieved was MicrosoftEdge.exe writing its own AppContainer DataStore/Recovery files on scranton at 03:21:05, which is normal Edge runtime behaviour, not credential theft.

findings.title: No password-manager artefacts observed
findings.summary: Checks C221-C226 returned zero hits: no KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass process executions, no .kdbx or password-manager file creation, no process-access events against password-manager processes, no command lines or script blocks referencing them, and no other-channel messages. The archive command on nashua (Rar.exe with -hpfGzq5yKw) and the *pass*/*login* file globbing are generic file collection, not password-manager store access.

findings.title: Network logons (4624 type 3) and explicit-credential logons (4648) are routine machine-account and PsExec activity
findings.summary: 218 event-4624 LogonType 3 records are dominated by machine account NEWYORK$ from ::1, fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 and 10.0.0.4 — normal local/loopback and DC machine-account authentication. The 15 event-4648 explicit-credential logons are pbeesly authenticating from 10.0.1.6 on scranton and via C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe on nashua, plus winlogon.exe DWM-1 logons; these are consistent with PsExec-based administration rather than a DC authentication backdoor. No 5136/4739 directory-service or policy changes were observed, so no evidence of modified domain-controller authentication.

findings.title: No password-filter DLL registration or System32 DLL drops observed
findings.summary: Checks for registry writes to Notification Packages / PasswordFilter / lsass keys (4657), process creation referencing Notification/PasswordFilter (4688), PowerShell referencing Notification/PasswordFilter/lsass (4104) and Sysmon file-create of DLLs in System32 all returned zero hits. The only authentication-DLL image loads seen are Microsoft-signed system DLLs (cryptdll.dll, samcli.dll, samlib.dll, msv1_0.dll) loaded by svchost.exe, WmiPrvSE.exe, SearchIndexer.exe, LogonUI.exe, dsregcmd.exe and lsass.exe itself — normal behaviour. No password filter DLL was installed.

findings.title: No reversible-encryption or account-flag modification activity
findings.summary: Queries for AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption / ReversibleEncryption in PowerShell script blocks (4104/4103), in Sysmon process command lines (Set-ADUser/dsmod/Reversible), in windows.other messages, and for event 4739 (domain policy change) all returned zero hits. No evidence that reversible password encryption was enabled.

findings.title: No MFA configuration or authentication-policy changes observed
findings.summary: Event 4739 (domain policy changed) returned zero hits, and no 5136 directory-service changes or Set-ADUser/Set-ADAuthenticationPolicy command lines were found in Sysmon or PowerShell. No evidence of MFA registration or MFA-bypass modification.

findings.title: No Network Provider DLL registration activity
findings.summary: Queries for registry writes (4657) to NetworkProvider/Credential keys and for PowerShell script blocks referencing NetworkProvider or New-ItemProperty returned zero hits. No network provider DLL was registered to capture credentials.

findings.title: No adversary-in-the-middle activity observed; hits reflect a separate credential-access/lateral-movement intrusion
findings.summary: The T1557 checks surfaced no AiTM positioning. Sysmon event.code 3 destination hostnames were uniformly '-' (1229/1229), DNS query names (81 events) contained only ordinary AD/DC discovery, Microsoft telemetry and update lookups, and the only 'wpad' lookups were routine wpad.dmevals.local queries answered NXDOMAIN by the domain controller 10.0.0.4 from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6. The two windows.other hits returned by the object-access/network checks were unrelated System-channel records (a Hyper-V miniport initialization and an RDP shell-start notification for DMEVALS\pbeesly from 172.18.39.2). What the data does show is a real intrusion on scranton.dmevals.local and nashua.dmevals.local by user pbeesly (SeaDuke-style PowerShell staging, PsExec64 with plaintext password to \\NASHUA, javamtsup service persistence, python.exe beaconing to 192.168.0.4:8443), but none of it is AiTM.

findings.title: No name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay; SMB traffic is legitimate PsExec admin-share use
findings.summary: No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay indicators were found. The 23 event.code 4697 service installations were almost all Windows per-user service registrations on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:20:48 (svchost.exe -k UnistackSvcGroup etc.) plus four PSEXESVC installs on nashua.dmevals.local by pbeesly and one javamtsup install on scranton.dmevals.local by pbeesly. The SMB share events (5140/5145) show only normal machine-account IPC$/SYSVOL/samr/lsarpc traffic to the DC newyork.dmevals.local and pbeesly's ADMIN$/IPC$ access from 10.0.1.4 to nashua.dmevals.local, i.e. the PsExec lateral movement, not a relayed authentication. The javamtsup service (C:\Windows\System32\javamtsup.exe, LocalSystem, auto-start) is malicious persistence but is not name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay.

findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning; MAC/IP mappings are stable and the odd responder MAC is a placeholder
findings.summary: Zeek conn records show only three source MACs (00:0d:3a:13:e3:69, 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2, fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and three responder MACs (12:34:56:78:9a:bc, 00:0d:3a:13:e3:69, ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff broadcast). The 12:34:56:78:9a:bc value is a synthetic/placeholder MAC, not a real host claiming multiple IPs, and it appears consistently as the responder for 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 traffic to 10.0.0.4 and 10.0.1.6. No duplicate MAC-to-IP mapping or gratuitous-ARP pattern is present, and no PowerShell script block referenced arp or netsh interface manipulation.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing indicators; no DHCP events or DHCP traffic in any dataset
findings.summary: The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP-related event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063 absent from the 216-event code stack), no PowerShell script block referenced DHCP, and Sysmon event.code 3 destination ports contain no 67/68 traffic (top ports were 8443, 389, 88, 53, 135, 445). The Zeek capture has no dhcp log type at all (only conn, files, ssl, x509, dce_rpc, http, dns, kerberos, dpd, smb_files, weird, smb_mapping, notice, pe), so DHCP spoofing is not observable and nothing suggests it occurred.

findings.title: No golden-ticket evidence: krbtgt service tickets are AES256 (0x12) for machine accounts only
findings.summary: All 28 Kerberos service-ticket requests (4769) on newyork.dmevals.local used Ticket Encryption Type 0x12 (AES256) with Ticket Options 0x60810010 and Failure Code 0x0 — no RC4 (0x17) downgrade typical of forged golden tickets. The three krbtgt service tickets were requested by pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL (23:04:04) and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL (23:19:13 and 23:19:15) from 10.0.1.4, consistent with normal machine-account TGT renewal; SCRANTON$ also logged on to newyork with Kerberos logon type 3 from 10.0.1.4. No 4672 special-privilege logon anomalies were found (the 212 events carry no TargetUserName value; sampled events show machine account NEWYORK$ with standard service privileges). No golden-ticket forging observed.

findings.title: No silver-ticket evidence: service tickets only for machine accounts, all AES256 and successful
findings.summary: The 4769 service-name distribution is NEWYORK$ (11), NASHUA$ (10), SCRANTON$ (3), krbtgt (3), WEC$ (1) — only computer accounts, no user service accounts with SPNs that would be targets of silver-ticket forging or service-ticket abuse. All requests succeeded (Status 0x0) with AES256 encryption and were issued by the KDC on newyork.dmevals.local, i.e. validated tickets, not forged ones. No silver-ticket behaviour observed.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting: no RC4 service-ticket requests and no roasting tooling in PowerShell logs
findings.summary: Kerberoasting requires TGS requests for SPN-bearing accounts returned with RC4 (0x17) encryption. All 28 4769 events show Ticket Encryption Type 0x12 (AES256) only, and the requested services are computer accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) plus krbtgt. PowerShell script-block searches for Kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/Rubeus returned zero hits, and the zeek Kerberos records (separate 2020-04-30 window) show only pbeesly AS/TGS requests for krbtgt, cifs/NEWYORK, ldap/NEWYORK, HTTP/NASHUA and cifs/NASHUA with aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96. No Kerberoasting observed.

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting: AS exchanges show normal pre-authentication
findings.summary: In the zeek Kerberos capture (2020-04-30, non-overlapping with the Windows window) the AS exchange from 10.0.1.4 for pbeesly/DMEVALS.LOCAL first returned KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED and then succeeded with aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96, i.e. pre-authentication is enforced — the opposite of an AS-REP-roastable account. PowerShell searches for AS-REP/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth returned zero hits. No AS-REP roasting observed.

findings.title: No forged web cookies observed; only benign INetCookies file creation and WebDAV DavSetCookie calls
findings.summary: The only cookie-related file creation in the window is C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-b484-4973-bbf2-a04208ecd4d4\AC\INetCookies created by svchost.exe on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:21:05, which is a normal per-package cookie store for a service profile. The only cookie-related process activity is rundll32.exe C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav (five executions on scranton at 03:08:50 and 03:10:22-23, parent svchost.exe), which is the standard WebDAV redirector setting a session cookie for a WebDAV share, not a forged authentication cookie. No PowerShell script block in the dataset references cookie, Set-Cookie or session (zero hits), and no browser cookie store was read or modified by the intrusion tooling.

findings.title: No SAML token forgery observed; certificate export is the closest precursor
findings.summary: No SAML assertion, NotOnOrAfter or Assertion strings appear in any PowerShell script block (zero hits), no process command line references saml/token/cert (zero hits), and no HTTP request in the Zeek window targets saml, adfs or token URLs (zero hits). The Zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window (2020-05-02), so web authentication traffic cannot be correlated with the host activity. The relevant precursor is the Get-PrivateKeys certificate/private-key export on scranton.dmevals.local, which could enable token-signing certificate abuse, but no forging or token use was observed in the retrieved data.

findings.title: No MFA/2FA request-generation activity observed; hits are benign WMI provider and authentication noise
findings.summary: Hunted for T1621 (MFA request generation / MFA fatigue) across windows.other, windows.security, windows.powershell, windows.sysmon and zeek. No MFA/2FA/authenticator/push/OTP-related script blocks, command lines, HTTP URLs or authentication-failure bursts were found. The only windows.other hits for the C355 check (event.code 5857/5858, 85 events) are WMI provider start/DeleteInstance records from wmiprvse.exe on newyork.dmevals.local (e.g. dsccore, CIMWin32, StorageWMI, WMIProv providers, all ResultCode 0x0 / 0x80041002 RSOP cleanup) — routine WMI/RSoP housekeeping, not authentication prompting. The single windows.security authentication-failure-family event is a successful NTLM credential validation (4776, Error Code 0x0) for pbeesly from workstation 10.0.1.4 on newyork.dmevals.local; no 4625 failures exist in the dataset. 4624 logons are ordinary Kerberos/Negotiate machine and user logons (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$, pbeesly, SYSTEM). The only sysmon process-creation hit for the C356 check was svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s TokenBroker on scranton.dmevals.local, a standard Windows service host. The zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows telemetry and contained no login/auth/mfa HTTP URLs. Separately, the same hosts do show unrelated hands-on-keyboard activity by user pbeesly (PsExec64 to \\NASHUA with a plaintext password, C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, sdelete64 wiping archives, hidden base64/gzip PowerShell on scranton.dmevals.local), which is credential-access-adjacent but is not T1621 and is out of scope for this technique family.

incidents.title: LSASS memory access with full-access masks by PowerShell on scranton and wsmprovhost on nashua
incidents.rationale: All these findings describe the same action: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff at 03:05:16Z, and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29Z. The full-access handle to LSASS memory is the classic credential-dumping pattern, best mapped to T1003.001 (LSASS Memory).

incidents.title: Keylogging and clipboard capture on scranton
incidents.rationale: pbeesly ran Get-Keystrokes with a Keystrokes job and read the clipboard. The primary input-capture action is keylogging (T1056.001).

incidents.title: Forced authentication via WebDAV/UNC coercion from scranton to 192.168.0.4
incidents.rationale: SMB attempts to 192.168.0.4 were rejected, then WebDAV requests with Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir were issued and answered 401 — coercion of authentication to an attacker-controlled server, matching T1187 (Forced Authentication).

incidents.title: Hidden PowerShell stager opened Microsoft Edge processes with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS
incidents.rationale: A hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell stager decoded a payload from monkey.png and opened Edge processes with 0x1fffff, consistent with in-memory browser session-cookie theft (T1539).

incidents.title: Unsecured credentials staged and exfiltrated via Invoke-Exfil on scranton
incidents.rationale: Invoke-Exfil compressed the Downloads directory (holding exported .pfx) into OfficeSupplies.7z and copied it to \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials; PsExec also used cleartext password. The credential-access element is unsecured credentials (T1552).

incidents.title: Credential-hunting file collection and plaintext credential use
incidents.rationale: pbeesly recursively enumerated the user profile for credential-bearing file patterns and archived them into working.zip, then Rar'd and sdelete'd them; also used plaintext passwords. The credential-access action is credentials in files (T1552.001).

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine certificate private keys to .pfx on scranton
incidents.rationale: All describe the same script block (Get-PrivateKeys, readme.ps1) enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and calling Export-PfxCertificate to write .pfx files protected by hardcoded password 'saribas'. This is private-key theft, T1552.004.

incidents.title: Credential/certificate theft tooling staged on scranton with no web-credential forging observed
incidents.rationale: Get-PrivateKeys exported certificate private keys and LSASS was accessed; the theft of authentication certificates maps to T1649 (Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates).

incidents.title: Low-confidence hostui.exe and sdclt.exe process anomalies on scranton
incidents.rationale: hostui.exe spawned by PowerShell and sdclt.exe spawned by cmd are process-execution anomalies (sdclt is UAC-bypass-capable), not observed credential access. Out-of-scope (T1036/T1548).

incidents.title: Attacker python.exe on nashua as C2/exfil client
incidents.rationale: The dropped python.exe unpacks a PyInstaller bundle and makes hundreds of outbound connections to 192.168.0.4:8443 — C2/exfiltration traffic, not network sniffing. Out-of-scope (T1071).

incidents.title: Sysinternals credential-access toolchain, PsExec lateral movement and anti-forensic cleanup by pbeesly
incidents.rationale: These findings cover staging of SysinternalsSuite, accesschk, PsExec64 with cleartext credentials against NASHUA, and sdelete64 wiping artifacts. The core observed action is lateral movement/execution via PsExec, not credential access, so it is out-of-scope (T1569).
